rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight peaks and identify critical pairs while targeting a short run. The low starting organic fraction preserves early retention, and the high endpoint promotes elution of strongly retained compounds.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to reveal which coeluting pairs respond to steepness. This should spread the crowded groups and establish whether temperature changes will also be needed.

The shallower gradient resolved all but one pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Raise temperature at the same slope to test whether selectivity separates the remaining close pair without sacrificing the other separations.

Test an intermediate temperature to open the near-coelution seen at 40 C without compressing the middle pair as much as at 55 C. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature selectivity and should retain a last-peak time below 10 minutes.

The temperature series suggests the critical middle pair crosses between 45 and 55 C, so moving to 60 C may widen its separation again. This should also improve the late close pair seen at 55 C and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.
Slightly flatten the gradient at the best temperature to improve the remaining R = 1.10 pair. The current last peak at 8.56 minutes leaves room for this change without incurring a time penalty.

The remaining close pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so shorten tG to move its separation in the favorable direction. This should bring that pair above R = 1.5 while testing whether the middle pair retains sufficient resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction slightly while preserving injection 7's gradient slope to test a small selectivity adjustment for the R = 1.46 pair. This also trims weak-solvent time while keeping ample retention for the first peak.

Use a slope between those of injections 7 and 5, retaining the higher starting fraction that improved the later close pair. This modest flattening should strengthen both crowded middle separations while preserving the later pair's resolution margin.

Slightly reduce the slope from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the marginal middle pairs above R = 1.5. The later close pair has enough margin for this small adjustment, and the last peak should remain well below 10 minutes.

Injection 10 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a slightly shallower gradient to shorten elution while attempting to preserve resolution of the three marginal pairs.

Injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark. Explore the cooler side of the near-coelution at 40 C, where reversing the temperature shift may separate that pair while preserving the other separations and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime using the solvent program of the maximum-score method. The larger temperature shift may move beyond the crossings seen at 35–40 C, while the higher starting organic fraction helps limit retention time; injection 10 remains the benchmark.

Raise temperature by one step from injection 13 to test whether the remaining close pair opens before another middle pair approaches coelution. This should shorten retention, while injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient in the low-temperature regime to improve injection 13's only unresolved pair while shortening retention. Injection 10 remains the established maximum-score method.

Continue the window adjustment that improved the low-temperature critical pair from R = 1.18 to 1.40 while shortening elution. A further increase in starting organic fraction with the same endpoint and duration may achieve full resolution; injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise temperature one step to improve the persistent R = 1.40 pair and shorten the run. The preceding pair now has more resolution margin than in the earlier 30 C experiment, making this a useful test of the narrower window.

Return to 25 C and flatten the gradient to test whether the remaining R = 1.40 pair can reach full resolution without a time penalty. The last peak at 8.75 minutes provides some headroom; injection 10 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Trim the low-temperature gradient window by raising the starting fraction one step, using injection 18's resolution margin to seek faster full separation. Its first peak is still well retained, so this is a reasonable test of reducing weak-solvent time.

Raise temperature one step from injection 19 to shorten the fully resolved low-temperature method. This tests whether its wider preceding-pair separation can accommodate the temperature shift while preserving all resolutions above 1.5; injection 10 remains the fastest maximum-score benchmark.

Return to the faster high-temperature regime and slightly flatten injection 11's gradient to improve its limiting middle pair. This tests a shorter alternative to injection 10 while retaining some margin in the later close pair.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction from the fully resolved injection 19 to shorten the low-temperature separation. Monitor the marginal middle pair closely; injection 10 remains the fastest method achieving the maximum CRF.

The middle pair approached a crossing as the starting fraction increased to 0.30; one further step tests whether it separates again in reversed order. This could yield a faster fully resolved method, while injection 10 remains the established maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting fraction one more step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation beyond injection 23. The first peak remains sufficiently retained to justify this test, while injection 23 is now the fastest established maximum-score method.

Shorten the gradient by one step from injection 24 to seek faster elution while testing whether the limiting R = 1.66 pair remains fully resolved. Injection 24 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if this change sacrifices resolution.
